text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The three-nation commission investigating the 1994 sinking of the Estonia ferry will critisise the crew in its final report, sources told the newspaper.

- Turbulence on the Stockholm bourse is continuing with the general stock market index falling 4.34 percent on Tuesday and 1.2 percent on Wednesday. This has created some uncertainty for new listings such as NK Cityfastigheter and Sardus.

- A dispute over wages by newspaper deliverers is over and services will return to normal after nearly two weeks of disruptions. From January 1 deliverers' hourly wage will be increased by 2.75 crowns, backdated, and from August 1 by a further 45 ore. The agreement is worth a rise of about four percent.
- Swedish households are increasingly optimistic about their own economies, according to the latest consumer confidence survey by Statistics Sweden.
- The City of Stockholm is to offer up to 10,000 school students summer jobs with wages of 40 crowns an hour. A spokesman for the City said it would be good work experience for the students.

- Nerves on the Stockholm bourse are expected to continue the rest of the week. In the past two days the bourse has slipped five percent with the drop larger than on other bourses in Europe. Two reasons are the fact the bourse has risen so much so far this year that profit takers are moving in and that interest rates have risen more in Sweden than overseas.

- The Swedish states aims to sell off its 25-percent stake in computer consulting company Enator by May 14 rather than by the end of March as previously announced. If the new target is not met the state's block of shares worth 1.4 billion crowns will be floated on the Stockholm stock exchange.

- Amerscan, a risk capital fund started by Norwegian Erik Tiller and American Marty Albert, has earmarked 320 million crowns for investments in small, Swedish information technology firms. One of the first Swedish firms to attract Amerscan's attention was IDS, Intelligent Documents System.

- Swedish oil and mining magnate Adolf Lundin, who controls companies listed in Toronto and Stockholm, has invested heavily in Zaire and Sudan, to the tune of 800 million crowns, even though both countries are currently torn by civil war. Lundin said forget politics, the world's largest deposit of copper is awaiting development in Tenke, a mining venture located in southern Zaire.
